codes.evidence_quote: The artistry and genius of Carlos Montoya have established him as without a rival in the world today and as probably the greatest of all gypsy guitarists of all time.
codes.rationale: The passage canonizes Montoya through superlative ranking and claims of unrivaled status.

codes.evidence_quote: Montoya showed himself to be a first-rate instrumentalist with a fiery musical temperament and a repertory of rare selections.
codes.rationale: The quoted review explicitly praises Montoya's instrumental quality, temperament, and repertoire.

codes.evidence_quote: San Diego Union's music critic, Donald Dierks -- known to be normally tough on guitarists
codes.rationale: The passage invokes named newspaper critics and their reviewing authority to authorize judgments of Montoya.

codes.evidence_quote: Montoya's early recordings reveal an interesting component of Gypsy-style, non-virtuoso flamenco; this was gradually replaced by a bag of crowd-pleasing tricks
codes.rationale: The passage evaluates Montoya's playing negatively as displaced by crowd-pleasing tricks.

codes.evidence_quote: Here's something Brook Zern writes in Guitar Review... And from Lives and Legends of Flamenco by D.E.Pohren
codes.rationale: The article authorizes its judgment by quoting recognized critical and flamencological sources.

codes.evidence_quote: It's not to take anything away from those who wish Montoya would preserve a purer flamenco style.
codes.rationale: The passage acknowledges a purity-based boundary by referring to a desired purer flamenco style, even while complicating its authority.

codes.evidence_quote: Montoya's playing is colorless, choppy, repetitious, boring, and sloppy. Everything sounds the same. There is nothing musical about it.
codes.rationale: The passage gives an explicit negative assessment of Montoya's musical quality.

codes.evidence_quote: he is one of the worst; in fact, only Manitas de Plata is worse. The contrast between Montoya's playing and that of Sabicas, Carlos Ramos, Diego del Gastor, Niño Ricardo, Mario Escudero, or Paco de Lucía, is stark.
codes.target: Montoya in relation to other flamenco guitarists
codes.rationale: The passage ranks Montoya near the bottom and constructs a hierarchy against named exemplary guitarists.

codes.evidence_quote: Yet those who know flamenco have no interest in seeing or hearing Montoya.
codes.target: Knowledgeable flamenco insiders versus mass audiences
codes.rationale: The passage draws an epistemic boundary between those who know flamenco and audiences persuaded by popularity or promotion.

possible_but_not_emitted.reason: The article uses insider critical authority, but this overlaps strongly with the emitted COMM_01 and CRIT_01 evidence.

codes.evidence_quote: Ramón Montoya, patriarch of the Montoya family and one of the important developers of the modern school of flamenco guitar playing
codes.target: Ramón Montoya and the modern school of flamenco guitar
codes.rationale: The passage canonizes Ramón Montoya as a patriarch and key developer of a major guitar school.

codes.evidence_quote: Ramón's playing was instrumental in the development of such guitarists as Luis Maravilla, Sabicas, and Mario Escudero
codes.target: Transmission from Ramón Montoya's playing to later guitarists
codes.rationale: The passage frames flamenco guitar knowledge as transmitted through influence across a lineage of players.

codes.evidence_quote: one can still recognize that he singlehandedly made the flamenco guitar a household word around the world and created an audience for the rest of us.
codes.rationale: The passage evaluates Montoya's significance by crediting him with creating a broad audience for flamenco guitar.
